subject: mushroomVillage
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: mushroom-house village.
Style: storybook illustration.
reasoning:
This is a mushroom-house village diorama, so I'm thinking through it as static scenery rather than a jointed creature. I'll aim for a reasonably scoped build—around 180-340 parts, a handful of textures, and roughly 600-800 lines of solid code.

I'm designing a round grassy base around 1.5m radius with an earthy soil skirt, then planning 4-5 varied mushroom houses with lathed stems and spotted caps, gill undersides, arched doors with decals, round glowing windows, chimneys, steps, lanterns, and mossy flower details, all built through a reusable house-generating helper.

I'm sketching a central tall "town hall" mushroom house with spiral shelf-fungus steps and a balcony, connected by a winding cobblestone path made of scattered flattened stones, bordered by a picket fence, lantern posts, a small lily-pad pond with a plank bridge, a signpost reading "MUSHROOM LANE," and clusters of flowers and grass tufts to fill out the scene.

I'm deciding to skip fireflies and trees for simplicity, adding a few small fern leaves instead, and leaning into a warm, painterly storybook style using the toon kit's two-tone cel shading as a base before pushing toward a softer gouache feel.

I'll build my own warm-top/cool-bottom paint helper with subtle mottle noise rather than relying on kits, importing only the glow kit for safety. Since I can't test live, I'm sticking to well-documented API calls like lathe, part, and extrude to avoid pitfalls.

This is a static model so joints can be omitted entirely, with parts placed directly via `at`. I also need to watch the 64-color limit, leaning on paints over flat colors, and keep the painted sheet texel density reasonable by sizing the paint canvas around 2048 for crispness given the total surface area.

For the mushroom cap spots, I'm weighing cell-based 3D paint spots against deliberately placed stick discs for a crisper storybook look — using surface placement on the lathe-generated cap, aiming for roughly 7-9 spots per house.

Settling on flattened disc geometry for each spot, seated slightly embedded into the cap surface and colored cream, distributed around the cap using azimuth/elevation placement.

I need rotation support so houses can face toward the path, so I'm building a local coordinate helper that handles position, rotated direction vectors, and scale together, with doors oriented to face +Z locally before rotating by yaw. Each house stem will use a lathe profile defined by radius/height points along its axis.

I'm sizing things out now: house bodies around 0.28-0.4m radius and 0.55-1.0m tall with caps up to 0.75m radius, keeping the whole diorama around 1.4m total height relative to a 1.5m base.

Now I'm working out the mushroom cap's lathe profile, defining the underside curve from the center axis out to the rim with a slight concave dip before flaring to the dome shape.

Continuing the loop up through the dome points to the apex, closing back along the axis, and keeping the axis corners marked sharp so smoothing doesn't push x negative during the lathe operation.

For the gill texture, I'm coloring the cap's underside based on the surface normal — where it points downward enough, I alternate between two gill colors using the angular coordinate to create radial stripe patterns, while the rest of the cap keeps its normal paint.

Still writing cap paint function...

Checking that mix, noise, paint, and smoothstep are all properly exported from the SDK, and confirming the underside normals behave correctly near the rim.

I'm deciding to keep the ground flat overall but add a grass-painted mound specifically under the big house, placing it slightly elevated with its own radius and height so the path can lead up to it with steps, and I'm working out a height function that blends the mound's falloff into the surrounding terrain.

The error's negligible, so I'll skip smoothing for mounds and just sink them slightly into the ground. I'm working out the base lathe profile with a soil skirt and grass lip, keeping the grass top flat at ground level with slightly rounded edges and enough segments for a smooth low-poly look.

For painting, I'm layering grass up top with soil bands below, embedding pebble cells for texture, and adding a zigzag drip edge where the grass overhangs the dirt for a storybook cutaway-earth look.

I also want a dark wooden plinth beneath the diorama, so I'm merging it into the same lathe profile—base rings slightly wider than the soil radius, with height bands that switch between plinth wood coloring and soil/grass coloring depending on y.

Setting GROUND to 0.2, and now mottling the top grass with varied green tones at a larger scale for texture.

For the path stones, I'm using flattened cylinders placed along a catmull-rom curve, sampling points manually to add lateral jitter rather than relying on the path's built-in frame callbacks.

To stay within part budget, I'm merging all the stone geometries into a single mesh using mergeGeometries from BufferGeometryUtils, applying a paint function that varies color per stone via a hash of cell id so they don't look uniform despite being one merged part.

For the static model without any joints, I'm leaving positioning as `at: [0,0,0]` and trusting parts default to the root when no bones exist, though I should verify static models can safely omit joints entirely.

Now I'm sketching the full element list: the plinth with soil and grass mounds, then six distinct houses. The first, a "Town hall," needs to be the tallest with a spotted red cap, a balcony ring with railing posts, a double round door, two rows of glowing windows, a chimney, a flag on a pole, and maybe a painted clock face or banner, with a spiral staircase of small half-disc steps winding up the stem to the balcony.

I'm diversifying the remaining five houses: a medium orange-cream cottage with a ladder and flower box, a tiny blue-purple fairy house with a lantern post, a tall skinny gold house with a crooked chimney and a hanging sign (bakery or post office with mailbox), a small pink spotted cottage, and a tiny teal toadstool home by the pond. Each gets a unique cap silhouette (flat, conical, bell-shaped) by varying the radius-to-height ratio, and I'm starting to think through how to build each stem using a lathe geometry for smooth tapering.

Now I'm working out the door details -- an arched extrude with a wood-grain paint, a slightly larger cream or brown frame, a gold knob sphere, and a tiny round window, then figuring out how to position it flush against the curved stem surface using a raycast to find the right embedding point.

I'm checking that the plate edges stay recessed relative to the curved surface at the given radius, accounting for thickness so the back face doesn't poke through while the front sits flush against the cylinder.

For the door, I'll extrude it with the center positioned at the surface point so the middle bulges slightly outward while edges stay close, paired with a slightly wider framing border.

For windows, I'm thinking of a round porthole design: a cylinder ring as the frame, a glowing warm-colored pane behind it, thin cross mullions, and possibly a textured decal suggesting curtains and light.

I'll generate a couple of SVG window textures—one round with a glowing glass gradient, curtain silhouette and a small plant, and another arched one with shutters—applied to flat planes with alpha cutouts so only the circular/arched shape shows, then make them emissive so they glow using the texture's own colors. I need to account for how a flat plane sits against a curved stem surface, since the plane only touches at its center and its edges will protrude slightly outward due to the curvature.

Rather than dealing with that gap, I'll switch to using decals that project directly onto the stem's curved surface, specifying a hit point and outward direction so the window texture wraps properly onto the geometry instead of floating above it.

Adding window shutters as small rotated boxes, then working out a helper to cast rays from the stem surface so I can place decals at precise points along the stem's height and angle.

For the chimney, I'm planning a tapered box cap with brick texture and a clay pot, plus small flattened spheres as stylized smoke puffs rising above in a gentle chain, keeping them subtle so nothing feels like it's awkwardly floating.

Now I'm working out placement: the chimney sits upright on the roof cap at a computed point, sunk slightly into the surface for a grounded look. I'll also add a small lantern post near the doors and a couple of flat half-step stones leading up to the entrance.

I'm adding small flourishes — flower boxes under windows with clustered colored spheres as blooms, a tiny mailbox post with a flag, and a door knob — then planning a pond scene with lily pads, reeds, a bridge, and a radially gradient water disc with ripple highlights computed from distance to center, surrounded by a ring of merged rim stones.

I'm also sketching a plank bridge with handrail posts, deciding pond placement by quadrant, and designing a picket fence helper that places posts and rails along a polyline path, plus a small pumpkin-and-cabbage garden patch for extra charm.

Now I'm scattering flowers randomly across the grass using a seeded RNG that rejects points too close to houses, paths, or the pond, then building merged geometries for thin stems and daisy-style flower heads grouped by color.

For grass tufts I'll use scattered cards with cross-facing geometry and slight random lean, textured with a three-blade gradient design, batched into one part for efficiency. I'm also planning small mushroom clusters using a toadstool helper that builds simple stem-and-cap geometries for scattered decorative placement.

For tiny mushrooms I can nest paints further, allowing a paint function to delegate to another paint for gills versus spots. Now thinking about the signpost at the path start — a wooden post with arrows pointing to "Bakery," "Town Hall," and "Pond," using thin textured boxes for the signboards since a box shows the drawing on all faces, though I'll need to figure out how to handle the arrow shape cutout.

I'm settling on using front-facing planes for the sign text so only the visible side shows lettering, keeping the back blank, with the arrow outline itself done as painted wood. Next I'm thinking through hanging bunting — a string of triangular flags strung between two points over the path.

For the bunting, I'm placing colored triangles along a catmull sag curve near a lamp post, sampling the path position and tangent at each point to orient small downward-pointing triangles with the tangent as the x-axis and thin extrusion thickness.

Thinking about other small touches now—skipping butterflies and ladybugs, but adding a cute snail near the pond with a spiral-swept shell and a capsule body, using a tapering spiral sweep for the shell shape with brown coloring.

For the body I'll use capsule shapes for tentacle rods plus eye spheres, keeping it around 10 parts total. Now I'm tallying textures: rounded windows, arched windows, grass tufts, three sign texts (bakery, town hall, pond), the snail spiral, and a door texture showing arched planks with hinges applied as a decal over the door extrude.

I realize the door texture can be drawn in greyscale and tinted per house using the color option, so each door's distinct color comes from tinting rather than needing separate textures—letting the arch's alpha cutout define the silhouette without extra geometry. So the door ends up as a dark wood frame extrude plus a tinted grey-plank decal layered slightly above the surface.

But the solid frame slab would completely cover the decal underneath it, so instead I'll make the frame a proper ring by sweeping a tube along the arch outline's path (straight sides up, semicircular top) with a small circular cross-section, giving a real 3D door-frame that sits around the door rather than behind it.

Figuring out exact surface placement is trickier since the door sits on a curved barrel-like stem — I need the radius profile at each height to compute the surface position, accounting for the lathe's polygon faceting, or alternatively just raycast each frame path point onto the stem surface to get accurate placement.

I'm setting up a raycasting helper that fires from local coordinates toward the stem and returns the hit point and normal, then using those hits to position decals with a slight outward lift so they sit just above the curved surface. The polygon faceting shouldn't cause visible issues for the decal projection. Now I'm planning out the full texture set — door, round and arched windows, tufts, signs, a snail, and a hanging banner with a mushroom emblem for the town hall.

I'm thinking through adding a flag emblem on a pole atop the town hall, maybe using two back-to-back texture planes so the mushroom crest is visible from both sides, bringing the texture count to around ten. I also want to scatter small glowing cyan toadstools near the pond as a whimsical touch, separate from any lantern or window glow effects, and I'm working out how the round window texture should render its frame and glass interior.

For the window decal, I'm making sure the frame stays non-glowing (since a glowing brown frame would look flatly bright) while the glass itself gets a warm yellow-orange gradient with dark cross bars and curtain silhouettes that glow appropriately. Now I'm defining the house spec type with fields for position, stem and cap dimensions, cap colors, and spot window properties.

I'll build one generic `house(spec)` function with flags for optional features like chimneys or balconies rather than separate functions per house type. For the layout, I'm working out absolute positions within the diorama radius, deciding the camera faces +Z, the path winds from the front toward a town hall at the back-center on a mound, and settling on direct meter-based dimensions for the town hall's stem and cap rather than a scale factor.

I'm sketching out positions, orientations, and stem/cap dimensions for each cottage—the orange one facing the path, the blue/purple fairy house, and the yellow bakery—using a helper to compute yaw so each door faces the right direction.

I'm continuing to assign sizes for the pink house with its chimney, and roughing out the pond location and path waypoints to make sure nothing overlaps.

Now I'm finishing the path, ending it at the raised mound near the town hall door, and planning small spur paths connecting the main route to each house's door.

I'm also checking the pond placement against house C's footprint—noticing a slight overlap and deciding to shift C's position to (1.0, 0.1) to keep clear separation.

Then I realize the base radius is too small: house D's cap would overhang the platform edge given its distance from center. I'm adjusting the overall base radius to around 1.85-1.9 to make sure every house footprint plus its cap stays within the boundary.

I'm repositioning each house slightly—D, E, B, and C—recalculating distance plus cap radius for each to confirm they fit within 1.75, then placing the town hall and pond with similar fit checks, and considering whether to add a small extra structure near the front-left pumpkin patch area.

I'm deciding five houses is plenty for the village, and considering adding a well as a charming prop—a stone cylinder base with a cobble texture, two support posts, a small red conical roof, and a bucket, positioned near the central path.

I also need an occupancy function to avoid overlapping scatter objects, factoring in house radii and the pond, and I'm thinking through whether decorative cards would awkwardly poke through if placed near the mound since the mound top sits above the base grass surface.

I'll exclude the mound area from scatter entirely and also keep clearance from the pond, well, path, and fences, computing sampled path points for distance checks. Estimating part counts, I land around 320 total objects across the base, mounds, houses, town hall, and props, with manageable triangle counts from the lathe geometry — now I'm ready to start writing the actual generation code.

Setting up imports and type-safe constants...

Defining more mounds...

Skipping that too. Now I'm working out the mound shape by lathing a radial profile—computing a parabolic height falloff from the outer edge down to the center axis, then building the outline points to loft into a 3D bump.

Writing grass paint shader...

Writing plinth and soil paint logic...

Finishing the local-to-world transform logic...

Now I'm writing a helper to scatter spots across the cap surface, using a golden-angle spiral for azimuth and varying elevation so spots cluster near the dome center, with randomized sizes for a natural look.

Now I'm placing the chimney on the cap using an upright cylinder with brick-colored stripe paint for courses, plus a darker pot ring and sphere puffs for smoke. Then I'm sizing the door opening with an arch frame, width and height scaled for the small structure.

Writing SVG arch texture...

I'll go with a single grey door texture, tinted multiplicatively per house color so the planks and hardware darken naturally. For windows I'll keep their own colored glow texture, and work out shutter placement by computing hit points along the wall surface and sticking boxes at the lateral offsets.

Writing shutter stick logic...

I'll keep it simple—skip the extra torus ring and just draw the window frame directly in the texture as a mid-brown outline, since emissive brightness matching the base color brightness will read naturally without needing separate geometry.

For the flower boxes under windows, I'm placing a small box plus a few spheres above it to form flowers, positioned using stick offsets along the window's hit point. The tricky part is generalizing the lateral stem positions so they work for windows at any angle, not just ones aligned with the door-forward axis.

Now I'm defining a helper that takes an angle and lateral offset, computes the outward direction by rotating forward, finds the origin point along the wall plus a lateral tangent shift, then casts inward to get the hit point -- using Vector3 math and a yaw-based rotation convention where positive angles rotate toward +X.

I'm sketching the stem's lathe profile as a series of radius/height pairs that taper and flare to suggest a mushroom stalk, then positioning the cap so its underside slightly overlaps the stem's top for a seamless join.

Good, so the stem top pokes slightly into the cap underside with no gap, confirming solid overlap. Now I'm working out the stem's paint function: a cream base with warm gradient variations by house, including mossy green near the bottom with zigzag texture, vertical grain streaks, and a darker shadow band where the cap overhangs near the top.

Still writing stem paint logic...

Adding rim trim coloring...

Now I'm figuring out window and decal placement on the stem, making sure the decal's orientation stays horizontal and outward-facing rather than following the sloped surface normal, so it looks stable regardless of the stem's profile curve.

Then I'm plotting the door frame as an arched sweep, building the point path for a semicircular arch by combining straight vertical sides with angled points along the curve.

For the knob I'm placing a small gold sphere near the top of the door, offset slightly outward from the surface normal, and the hinges are handled by texture rather than geometry. Finally I'm starting to add a couple of flat stone steps leading up to the doorway.

I'm using heightAt per position so house bases sink slightly into the mound surface, and off-mound houses sit at a fixed sunken depth. Now I'm writing a lamp helper that places a post at ground height with a glowing lantern box, a dark cap, and a small side arm for hanging.

Now I'm figuring out placement of two lamp posts near the path and pond, then planning bunting strung between their tops across the path gap.

Extending the path toward the town hall and mound, checking how it merges with the mound's rising terrain near the stone steps at the door. I'm working out stone placement along the path—spacing them by arc length with randomized size and lateral jitter so they look naturally scattered rather than perfectly aligned.

Still writing stone placement logic...

I'll write a helper function that places stones along a path with position, radius, and yaw, merging each colour group's cylinder geometries into one combined part with scaling and rotation applied per stone. Then I'm defining the pond as a flattened cylinder shape with its own water paint material at a set position and radii.

For the water material, I plan to shade it as a gradient based on radial distance from the pond's center, going from a deep blue-green core to a lighter edge, layering in ripple rings and sun glints since the top face normal points upward. I'm also adding a ring of merged rim stones around the pond's ellipse edge plus a darker muddy ring beneath the water surface for depth.

Now I'm adding lily pads as flattened green discs with slight color variation, plus a small cluster of pink lotus flowers made from tilted cone petals arranged in a radial pattern, angled outward and upward from the center.

Then I'm placing reeds and cattails around the pond edge using leaning spikes for the grassy stems, topped with small brown capsule shapes for the cattail heads.

Now for the bridge, I'm designing a small arched footbridge crossing the pond's narrow axis, built as a bezier sweep path with a raised control point for the arch and a box-shaped cross-section for the deck.

I'm adding plank-style paint striping along the bridge deck for visual texture, then working out the railings — sampling points along the bridge path to place posts on both sides with an offset top rail sweep running parallel to the deck.

Checking whether the path's `.at(t)` returns a plain Vector3 so I can rely on arc-length sampling for railing and post placement. Now I'm shifting focus to building a stone well: a lathed cylindrical body with a hollow inner wall so I can fit a water disc inside it.

Writing shell wall outline...

Still building roof details...

Now I'm adding a small pumpkin patch nearby, using squashed spheres painted orange with subtle radial ribbing to suggest pumpkin ridges, figuring out how to center that ribbing pattern around each pumpkin's vertical axis.

I decide to switch to low-poly faceted spheres (8 width, 5 height segments, flat shading) so the lobes naturally read as ribs without extra math, coloring them crisp orange with tiny green stem cylinders on top, and planning similar green spheres for cabbages nearby. Then I sketch a raised garden bed: a fenced rectangular plot with dark furrowed soil, rows of cone-topped carrots, and the pumpkins sitting on top, positioned off to the side with a slight rotation.

Writing fence helper code...

I work out the yaw angle from the direction vector using atan2, confirming all box and cone geometries share the same attribute set so they can be merged. For the signpost, I'm planning the post, arrow-shaped extruded boards, and text planes, defining the arrow outline points and thickness, with text positioned on the board.

Working out thickness axis math...

Working through the signpost orientation: the sign face should front toward the viewer (+Z), with its arrow direction aligning with the viewer's sense of right/left, so dirV=(1,0,0) corresponds to pointing rightward from the viewer's perspective standing near the path start.

I'll also add a small yaw angle ψ so the sign can tilt slightly, recomputing the thickness axis via cross product to keep it facing correctly, then move on to generating the text texture using an SVG with serif text.

For the signpost labels I'll make three boards: "TOWN HALL", "BAKERY", "POND", while the bakery's hanging sign will use a separate bread/croissant icon texture rather than reusing the text, hung from a bracket arm with little chain details.

Tallying textures needed so far: door, round window, arch window, tuft, three signs, snail, bread icon, and an emblem flag—roughly ten or eleven total.

For the town hall I'm adding a balcony ring with a wood-painted disc and railing made from post cylinders and a closed circular sweep for the top rail.

Above that I'm placing two arched upper windows plus the balcony itself, skipping a second door or bell idea. Then I'm designing a spiral staircase of bracket fungi climbing from the ground to the balcony—seven angled half-disc steps jutting from the stem at increasing heights and angles, painted in orange fungal colors, starting near the door and winding upward.

Now I'm adding a round decorative clock face above the door, positioning it so it sits just above the balcony railing without overlapping, plus two round windows flanking it at angled positions.

I'm figuring out the flag pole and emblem on the cap top, using a ray hit to find the cap's top surface so I can place the pole, swallowtail flag, and twin chimneys correctly. I'm also sketching out generic house-building flags like chimney, balcony, hangSign, flowerBoxes, lamp, and stairs to parameterize the house generator.

Now I'm defining color palettes per house variant—red tones for the town hall, orange for house B, purple-blue for house C, yellow for house D, each with base, light, dark, and spot accent colors for the cap paint.

I'm also sketching smaller decorative elements: little toadstools, glowing lamp and cap colors, and grass tuft SVGs with gradient blades from dark base to light tip.

Now I'm scattering details across the base mesh, weighting the distribution by surface area so more land on top than on the sides or bottom, with a filter requiring upward-facing normals and spacing checks to avoid overlap.

For flowers, I'm building thin cylindrical stems topped with squashed sphere heads, grouping them by color into merged geometries—stems green, petals in a few hues, tiny gold centers for the daisy-like ones.

For greenery, I'm adding flat-shaded icosahedron bushes scattered around with small berry accents, and considering small details like a lamp post and a snail placed near the path edge, keeping extras minimal to avoid overcomplicating the scene.

Still writing snail geometry...

For the back circle, I'm just flipping the facing direction so the texture mirrors but the spiral still reads fine — drawn as a dark brown spiral on orange fill, with alpha cutoff below 0.5 for clean edges. For decoration I'm picking bunting colors (red, yellow, teal, pink) and designing the town hall's flag as a cream swallowtail banner with a mushroom emblem painted on both sides.

I'm defining the swallowtail outline points for the flag shape and planning the pole with a gold ball finial on top. I'm also considering a small gill-skirt ring under the cap rims for extra detail, though some other embellishments like moss tufts I'll skip for now.

This is a classic amanita-style ring, so I'll add it to the town hall and buildings B and E, placing it around y = sh*0.88 and keeping windows at mid-height to avoid clashing. Now it's time to actually write the code, starting with helper functions like degree conversion and vector construction utilities.

Setting up imports...

Still writing SVG code...

Finishing the door with plank lines, hinges, and a porthole window, then moving to a grass tuft SVG with multiple curved blades in varying shades of green.

Now I'm planning the sign text generator with centered bold serif lettering sized to fit the label, a simple bread loaf illustration, and a mushroom emblem with a spotted cap and stem.

For the clock face I'm laying out a cream circle with a ring, tick marks, and hands at 10:10, then working out a spiral shell path for the snail using curved arc segments.

Now I'm building the base using a lathe profile, defining the radial and vertical points for the outline and checking that the shape won't self-intersect, with segment count and color settings applied.

I'm working out the paint logic based on height and normal thresholds -- deciding where the wood of the plinth ends and where soil versus grass coloring takes over near the lip, blending normals to smooth the transition.

I'm also setting up a tiling noise helper for texture variation, then using a cell-based scattering function to place rounded stone shapes into the soil surface, coloring them with mixed earthy tones and darker outlines based on cell distance values. I'm layering this with banded earth coloring that blends two brown tones using a smoothstep on vertical position plus noise for a more natural dirt look.

I'm reconsidering the proportions of the base: the soil layer above the plinth felt too thin, so I'm bumping up the GROUND constant to 0.24 for a thicker, more substantial base while keeping the wood plinth around 0.06 tall.

I'm now laying out the overall build order: constants and texture/paint setup first, then the base and mounds, followed by path computation and stone placement, then houses, then the various props like the well, pond, bridge, lamps, bunting, signpost, fencing, bushes, toadstools, flowers, and snail, and finally merging everything and returning the root group.

For the houses, I need each door's position before building spurs — computing it as the house position plus a forward offset for the step area, then routing a short wobbly path from the nearest main path point to that door. I'm working out yaw angles for each house so their doors face toward specific target points (town hall faces straight ahead at yaw 0, house B angles around 1.2 radians, house C mirrors at -1.2, and house D needs its own angle toward a point near the hall mound), defining a specs table with position, facing target, and derived orientation for each building.

I'm checking that house D and E sit near the edge of the hall mound, and realizing the ground slope there is steep enough that opposite sides of a house's stem could differ in height by nearly 0.17 units — meaning I need to sample heightAt() carefully per-point rather than just using the center height, or the houses will look tilted or floating on one side.

Reducing D's cap to .46 gives a small margin at 1.79, so I'll just enlarge R to 2.0 instead to give more breathing room — that keeps all positions, the pond, and base radius sizing comfortably within bounds.

Setting houses D, E, B, C at specific coordinates around the enlarged base, then working out which areas count as "taken" — the houses' footprint, the town hall mound, pond ellipse, well, garden rectangle, and path corridors — so I can keep everything else clear for placement.

Writing stone-laying function...

Stones get grouped into three sets and built as scaled, rotated cylinders positioned at their height-adjusted spots, with spurs lining up to step positions. Now I'm moving on to writing the house-building function, starting with defining the shape of a house spec.

Defining house-building logic...

Defining point types for outline arrays...

For stem faceting, I'm weighing lower segment counts like 10 for a subtly faceted, storybook look since the paint texture will hide hard edges, and checking whether a door decal centered on a facet vertex would awkwardly straddle a corner rather than sitting flush.

I'll go with 12 smooth-shaded segments for the stem instead. Now I'm defining the cap lathe profile with its lip and rounded crown shape, setting the cap's position, segment count, and smoothing, then double-checking that the underside lip points and loop winding give correct normals.

For the cap paint function, I'm using the surface normal and noise to detect gill regions on the underside, then shading gills darker toward the stem center using radial distance from the house origin, mixed with cream tones.

I'm also adding a thin cream rim trim at the lip edge using normal angle thresholds, a soft highlight on the top using a smoothstep on the upward normal, and placing cap spots offset above the cap surface for added texture.

Now I'm working out the collar geometry and paint color between the cap and stem, then figuring out the door's tangent vector by rotating the forward direction ninety degrees to get a perpendicular placement.

I'm computing the ray origin and direction for door placement using the lateral offset, checking against the stem's surface via a ray cast that throws if there's no hit, then setting the door's width and height dimensions proportional to the stem radius with a minimum size.

I'm defining the door decal placement using a hit point and forward direction, with dimensions and a slight lift, then working out the arch-shaped frame geometry for the door's rounded top.

I'm handling edge cases where the ray hits near the stem base, nudging the y-value to avoid degenerate hits at the boundary, and offsetting surface hits slightly along the normal. For the frame color, I'm leaning toward a cream-white tone like "#fbf1d8" to match a storybook door aesthetic rather than dark wood.

I'm adding a small gold sphere for the door knob positioned relative to the door's height and width, offset along the surface normal. Then I'm working out the step geometry below the door—computing each step's position along the forward direction from the stem base, with radius and thickness decreasing per step, placed using tapered cylinders at the correct height.

For the stone material, I'm defining a mottled paint pattern blending tan tones for texture. I'm widening the hall to use three steps instead of two.

Now I'm setting up window placement—defining a generic window spec with angle, height, kind (round or arch), and size, then writing a helper function that computes the window's position and orientation, adds a decal shaped like the chosen window type, and applies a glow effect to make it stand out.

I'm also adding a torus-shaped frame ring for round windows, plus shutter sticks on either side, and thinking through how the ring's slight offset might cause it to float or sink against the curved stem surface depending on the facet geometry.

For the decal glow and shutters, I'm confirming the material handling works fine for textured (non-painted) decals. I'm also sketching out a flower box option beneath the window—a sunken wood box sized to the window width with small sphere flowers arranged along its length.

I'm adding a flattened green box for foliage sitting atop the flowers, then setting up a lamp post helper positioned relative to the door with a side offset. I'm starting the chimney logic as a surface built when the chimney option is specified.

Still working out chimney geometry...

Using low-poly spheres for the lamp geometry, then defining a lamp post function and a balcony ring attached to the house stem at a scaled radius near the base.

Posts become 16 thin merged cylinders along the ring. I'm double-checking clock clearance above the rail and considering whether to add a small arched balcony door near the back, though I might skip it to keep things simple.

For the small round windows at either side I'm placing them slightly overlapping the rail, which works fine visually. Then I'm working out the stair geometry — seven steps spiraling from front-right to the balcony, computing each step's angle and height so the last one lands exactly at the balcony level, and figuring out how to shape each step as a half-cylinder disc.
